newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan fears FCC plan may snarl telecom talks.
newsitem.headline: Japan fears FCC plan may snarl telecom talks.

text.p: A U.S. proposal to force foreign phone companies to cut rates they charge U.S. carriers for calls from the United States could snarl efforts to forge a global telecoms pact by a February deadline, a Japanese government official said on Friday.

"If the U.S. rule is not on a Most Favoured Nation (MFN) basis, it would hamper the WTO (World Trade Organisation) process for an agreement," a Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications official told reporters.
Negotiations under the WTO will reopen next month in an effort to meet the February 15 deadline for a deal to free up the world's $500 billion basic telecommunications market.

An original April deadline was missed after Washington -- under heavy pressure from U.S. industry -- deemed that a "critical mass" had not been achieved to a degree sufficient to justify the United States opening up its own market to all comers.
The talks resumed this autumn and got a boost in November when Washington and Brussels put new packages on the table.

In a plan unveiled on Wednesday, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) proposed setting "benchmarks" to try to push down so-called "settlement rates" levied to complete calls originated in the United States.
The upper limit would be 15 cents per minute for high-income countries, 19 cents per minute for middle-income countries, and 23 cents per minute for low-income countries.
Japan would also like to see lower settlement rates, since its carriers have to pay hefty sums to developing countries' carriers, the official said.
But Tokyo is worried that the new "benchmark" system could act as a barrier to entry by foreign firms to the U.S. market.
"Philosophically, we are on the same line as the U.S. -- we would like to see prices go down and lower (settlement) rates. The difference is over how to achieve that."
"We still don't know the details of the (FCC) proposal. Our concern is whether the new proposal is really MFN or is a disguised barrier to market entry," the official added.
Informal telecom talks last week on the fringes of the WTO's first ministerial meeting in Singapore helped boost momentum to meet the February 15 deadline, the official said.

But he added that the outlook for successful conclusion of a deal hinged both on the acceptability of the new U.S. proposal and on the improvement of liberalisation offers by other countries, especially developing Asian economies.

Tokyo, for its part, says it has made its own best offer, including the planned removal of limits on foreign ownership other than a 20 percent restriction on foreign stakes in international carrier KDD (Kokusai Denshin Denwa Co Ltd) and domestic giant NTT (Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp).
"Our understanding is that we made our best offer in April and in fact there is no room to make more improvements," the official said.
